Files: template.html (the page: abcjs 6.5.2 from CDN renders ABC notation and plays it through ABCJS.synth.SynthController, which is loaded into a hidden #synthHost and driven by the page's own buttons), build.js (`node build.js` inlines pieces/*.abc into dist/player.html), cdp.js (a tiny Chrome DevTools driver; there is no npm and no `lor browser`, so use this with the installed chrome-headless-shell), test-player.js (`node test-player.js` opens file://quartet/dist/player.html, clicks play, pauses, resumes, prints state each second).

2. The test read quartetDesk.synth().midiBuffer.audioBuffers[0] and got peak=0.000, rms=0. Find out whether the audio is really silent (for example the soundfont notes from https://paulrosen.github.io/midi-js-soundfonts/abcjs/ did not load, or the instrument override in sequenceCallback breaks note loading) or whether that measurement is wrong. 4. For programs 40, 41, 42 and 48, measure how a long note behaves in this soundfont: play one 4-second note and report the amplitude envelope (time to reach peak, level at 1s, 2s, 3s, 4s). Say whether long notes die away early. If they do, check whether the FluidR3_GM or MusyngKite variants at the same host sustain better, and report numbers; do not switch the soundfont yourself.

Keep the code simple. When done, reply with: what was wrong, what you changed (file and function), and the test output that shows each item working. Mark anything you could not verify.

entries.text:
The player exists; the music doesn't yet. What's above is only a four-bar test fragment I wrote to exercise the page, not the composition.

**Working (checked in a headless browser):** the score engraves from text, and pressing play moves the cursor and clock through the bars.

**Not working or not verified:**
- **Sound:** I can't confirm any comes out. My one measurement of the audio buffer read as silent, and I don't know yet whether that's a real problem or a bad measurement.
- **Pause then resume:** the page says it's playing but the cursor stays frozen.
- **Seek, tempo, sound choice, part mutes, downloads:** built but untested.

If you press play above, telling me whether you hear anything would settle the sound question quickly.

A [subagent](in-app link omitted) is fixing and testing playback now. When it reports back I'll start on the piece itself.

The plan for the piece is a compact sonata-form first movement in D minor, a key Beethoven never used for a quartet. I'm writing it in ABC notation, a standard text format for scores that the page can both engrave and play, and that exports to MIDI.

I can't hear, so I'll check the writing by analysis (bar lengths, instrument ranges, the harmony on each beat, parallel fifths), and you'll be the judge of how it sounds.

entries.speaker: Lor
entries.text:
It was my bug, and the copy above has a stopgap fix: it now plays as solo strings, so press play again.

**Why it was silent:** the Sound menu (solo strings / string section / piano) worked by swapping each part's instrument just before the audio was built. The player library had already fetched samples for the original instruments by then, so every note pointed at an instrument with nothing loaded and was skipped.

**What I changed:** I removed that swap and disabled the Sound menu until it's done properly. In a headless browser the audio buffer now has a real signal (peak 0.92, where it was 0.00 before).

I still can't confirm what you'll hear in the app itself, so tell me if it stays silent on your side. Pause-then-resume is still broken in this copy; the subagent is fixing that and the Sound menu in the real source.

entries.text:
All four items are fixed or measured. The page now plays, pauses and resumes correctly, and every Sound option produces real audio. I changed only `template.html` and rebuilt `dist/player.html`. Nothing under `pieces/` changed, nothing visual changed, and no artifacts were published.

## What was wrong and what I changed (all in `template.html`)

1. **Resume did nothing.** abcjs's `play()` is a toggle that flips an internal "started" flag. The page paused with `pause()`, which leaves that flag set, so the next `play()` paused again.
   - **Fix:** `togglePlay()` now pauses by calling `synthControl.play()`.

2. **The audio really was silent, and the measurement was right.** The soundfont was not at fault. The instrument override in `sequenceCallback` broke note loading, for two reasons:
   - abcjs picks which samples to download from the tune's own `%%MIDI program` lines before `sequenceCallback` runs.
   - Inside the callback the instrument is a name like `"violin"`, and the page wrote numbers over it.

   abcjs's debug log showed `placeNote skipped (instrument empty): 40` for every note. Writing names instead fixed solo, but section and piano stayed silent because their samples had never been downloaded.
   - **Fix:** removed `sequenceCallback` from `audioParams()`. A new `overridePrograms()` (called from `engrave()`) sets the programs where abcjs builds the sequence, before it chooses samples.

3. **Found while testing seek: audio and cursor drifted apart.** After any seek during playback (slider, note click, or the tempo change's own internal seek), abcjs keeps an old start time. The next pause/resume then restarted the audio several seconds behind the cursor: audio at 4.51s while the clock showed 0:11.
   - **Fix in `seekTo()`:** while playing, it pauses, seeks, then resumes.
   - **Fix in the tempo `change` handler:** while playing, it pauses, changes the tempo, then resumes. A paused piece now stays paused instead of showing "stopped". A tempo change made while another is still in progress is applied when that one finishes.

4. **Small fix:** `onFinished` now resets the clock to `0:00 / total`. It used to stay at `0:16 / 0:16`.

## Test output
I added two test scripts:
- `test-features.js` puts a probe on the audio output to measure what is actually playing (`liveRms`), and records where the audio really is (`audioPos`).
- `test-envelope.js` measures long notes.

1. **Resume did nothing.** abcjs's `play()` is a toggle that flips an internal "started" flag. The page paused with `pause()`, which leaves that flag set, so the next `play()` paused again.

entries.text:
The first 25 bars are above and should play: about a minute of music, a slow introduction and then the first theme of the Allegro.

- **Bars 1–8, Poco sostenuto:** a four-note cell (A, B♭, down to C♯, D) enters in the cello, then viola, second violin and first violin in turn. It swells to an augmented-sixth chord and falls back to a quiet dominant.
- **Bars 9–16, Allegro agitato:** the same cell fortissimo in bare octaves, answered quietly; then again a fourth higher, turning toward G minor.
- **Bars 17–25:** the first violin takes off over pulsing inner parts, climbs to a Neapolitan E♭ and closes firmly in D minor.

I checked it by analysis only: bar lengths, instrument ranges, the chord on every beat, and no parallel fifths or octaves. How it sounds is for you to judge.

The player's pause/resume, seek, tempo, Sound menu and part mutes are now fixed and tested in a headless browser. It also retries a note sample that fails to download.

Two limits of the sampled strings will affect what you hear:
- **Slow attack:** each note takes about a second to reach full level, so the fast pulsing eighths in the Allegro may sound soft or blurred.
- **Long notes cut off:** a held note goes silent after about 6 seconds, so I keep notes shorter than that.

Overnight I'll write the rest of the movement: transition, a second theme in F major, development, recapitulation and coda. I'll republish to this same artifact as each section passes the checks; the cover line says how far it has got and when. The page doesn't refresh itself, so reopen [the artifact](in-app link omitted) to get the newest copy. Sleep well.

command:
cd ~/quartet && ./publish.sh 2>&1 | tail -2 && mkdir -p briefs && cat > briefs/common.md <<'EOF'
# Shared brief: String Quartet in D minor, "in the manner of Beethoven"

The user heard a concert, wants "more Beethoven string quartets", and asked for a full four-movement quartet by morning. I (the lead agent) am writing movement I. You write ONE other movement, complete, on your own, in the file named in your task. Work in quartet/.

## What exists
- `pieces/01-dminor-i.abc`: movement I (in progress). READ IT FIRST and copy its conventions exactly: header fields, the four `V:` lines, `%%score [1 | 2 | 3 | 4]`, the `%%MIDI program` preamble after `K:`, one line per voice per system written as `[V:1] ... |`, `%` comment lines naming each section with bar numbers, and the two first lines `%%label` (short name for the menu) and `%%note` (one sentence of programme note shown on the page).
- `check.js`: `node check.js pieces/<file>.abc` must end with `no problems found`. It checks bar lengths, that all four voices have the same number of bars, instrument ranges, and parallel fifths/octaves between any two parts (sampled every eighth note). `node check.js pieces/<file>.abc --chords --from 9 --to 16` prints the sounding notes on each beat, bottom part first; use it to confirm the harmony is what you intended. It is my substitute for ears, so use it constantly.
- The page that engraves and plays the files is abcjs 6.5.2. I build and publish; you do not.

## The quartet
- Key D minor. Middle-period Beethoven idiom (Op. 59, Op. 74, Op. 95): motivic concision, real four-part writing, dialogue between the instruments, sudden dynamic contrasts, off-beat sforzandi, silences, clear cadences and phrase structure, a real bass line. Original themes only: do not quote Beethoven or anyone else.
- The whole quartet grows from one four-note cell stated in the slow introduction of movement I: A, B flat, down a diminished seventh to C sharp, D (scale degrees 5, flat 6, raised 7, 1: semitone up, diminished seventh down, semitone up). Its major-mode form is 5, 6, 7, 1 rising by step. Your movement should use the cell or a clear transformation of it somewhere that matters (a theme head, a bass figure, a climax), not as decoration.

## Hard rules for the notation
- `L:1/8`. One meter for the whole file (check.js reads only the first `M:`). No pickup bar: start with rests inside a full first bar.
- Repeats: plain `|:` and `:|` only. No first and second endings. Write a da capo out in full.
- Tempo: `Q:"Italian marking" 1/4=NN` (or `3/8=NN` etc.). A tempo change inside the piece is an inline `[Q:"..." 1/4=NN]` in voice 1 only.
- Put every dynamic mark in all four voices (the player leaks a dynamic from one voice into the others if a voice has none). Use `!pp! !p! !mp! !mf! !f! !ff! !sfz!`, `!fermata!`, slurs `( )`, staccato `.`, `!trill!` sparingly.
- Accidentals: the key signature applies; an accidental lasts to the end of the bar in that octave; restate it after a barline. Mid-piece key signature change: inline `[K:D]` in all four voices at the same barline.
- Ranges: violins G3 (`G,`) up to about F6 (`f'`), exceptionally higher; viola C3 (`C,`) up; cello C2 (`C,,`) up. Middle C is `C`; `c` is the C above; `C,` the C below.
- Double stops `[F,A,]` are allowed but keep them rare and easy (thirds, sixths, octaves with an open string).
- Sound limits of the player: a note goes silent about 6 seconds after it starts, so no note or tied note may last longer than about 5 seconds at your tempo; re-articulate instead. Bowed samples swell slowly, so very fast notes sound soft: do not build the movement on runs of sixteenths.
- Parallel octaves that are deliberate doubling (a unison passage, two instruments in octaves on a melody for a whole phrase) are accepted by the checker when the doubling lasts; otherwise fix every flagged parallel, including those between a rocking accompaniment and a melody.

## How to work
1. Plan first, in writing for yourself: form with bar counts, keys, the themes as actual notes, the harmony bar by bar.
2. Write four to eight bars at a time for all four parts, run check.js with `--chords` on those bars, fix, go on. Do not write the whole movement before the first check.
3. Compose real music: phrases that breathe and cadence, inner parts that move, the melody passed around, the cello sometimes singing, contrast between sections, a climax, an ending that is prepared. Avoid: block chords for pages, the first violin always on top with a tune, endless sequences, a harmony that never leaves tonic and dominant.
4. Finish the whole movement to the last bar. A complete, sound movement of modest length beats an ambitious torso.

## Do not
- Edit any file except your own piece file (and scratch files under /tmp). Not check.js, template.html, build.js, publish.sh or other pieces. If check.js misbehaves on something legitimate, say so in your report instead of patching it.
- Run the browser tests or publish artifacts.

## Report back (short)
The file path; the form as a list of sections with bar numbers and keys; tempo and approximate duration; the final `node check.js` line; anything you are unsure about musically.
EOF
cat > briefs/ii.md <<'EOF'
Read quartet/briefs/common.md first and follow it.

Your movement: II, the slow movement. File: quartet/pieces/02-dminor-ii.abc

- Adagio (your choice of exact marking, e.g. "Adagio molto espressivo"), B flat major, the key a third below D minor. 3/4 or 4/4. Tempo slow enough to be a true adagio but respect the 5-second note limit (for example 1/4=52 to 58).
- Character: a hushed, hymn-like theme in the low and middle register (think of the slow movements of Op. 59 no. 2 and Op. 74 for the kind of thing, not for the notes), sustained, with a long-breathed melody. This kind of writing is what the sampled strings do best.
- Form: either a theme with two or three variations and a coda, or a broad A B A' with coda. In either case the middle should darken (B flat minor or G minor) and bring the cell in its true minor form (in B flat minor: F, G flat, down to A, B flat) as an intrusion, and the return should be decorated (flowing eighths or triplet-like figuration in an inner part or the first violin, the melody given to another instrument such as the cello in its tenor register).
- The theme itself can be related to the major form of the cell (5, 6, 7, 1 rising by step) or to its opening semitone.
- Ending: pianissimo, on B flat major, with a last quiet reminder of the cell.
- Length: about 60 to 90 bars, 4 to 6 minutes.
EOF
cat > briefs/iii.md <<'EOF'
Read quartet/briefs/common.md first and follow it.

Your movement: III, the scherzo. File: quartet/pieces/03-dminor-iii.abc

- Scherzo: Allegro molto (or Presto), D minor, 3/4 felt one in a bar. Trio in D major (key change `[K:D]`), then the scherzo again written out in full, then a short coda.
- Character: terse, rhythmic, a little grim and witty: a short rhythmic motive tossed between the instruments, off-beat sforzandi, sudden pianos, bars of silence, hemiolas. Build it from the cell (A, B flat, C sharp, D) compressed into the scherzo rhythm. The trio should contrast: warm, rustic, legato, perhaps a drone or a tune in the viola or cello with the others accompanying, using the major form of the cell.
- Form: scherzo ||: a :||: b a' :|| ; trio ||: c :||: d c' :|| ; scherzo da capo written out without repeats; coda. Plain repeat signs only, no first and second endings: shape the last bar of each repeated section so it leads both back and on.
- Because fast bowed notes sound soft in the player, get the energy from quarter notes, rests, accents and register, not from running eighths.
- Tempo suggestion: 3/4 with `Q:"Allegro molto" 3/4=84` or thereabouts if abcjs accepts a dotted-half beat; otherwise `1/4=252`. Check with check.js that the file parses, and say in your report which you used.
- Length: about 3 to 4 minutes with repeats (roughly 48 to 64 bars of scherzo, 32 to 48 of trio, the da capo, 8 to 16 of coda).
EOF
cat > briefs/iv.md <<'EOF'
Read quartet/briefs/common.md first and follow it.

Your movement: IV, the finale. File: quartet/pieces/04-dminor-iv.abc

- Finale: Allegro (your marking, e.g. "Allegro con fuoco" or "Allegretto agitato" in the manner of the Op. 95 and Op. 132 finales), D minor, 2/4 or 6/8, ending with a faster coda in D major (key change `[K:D]`, inline tempo change) in which the cell appears in its major form (A, B, C sharp, D rising) as a release.
- Form: a rondo or sonata-rondo: A (refrain, D minor) B (F major or A minor) A C (a developmental or contrapuntal episode: a short fugato on the cell A, B flat, C sharp, D would be very much in style) A, then the D major coda. Write the refrain so that its returns can be varied a little (scoring, register, dynamics) rather than copied blindly.
- Character: restless, driven, a dance-like or galloping refrain with a memorable rhythm; a lyrical or hymn-like contrast for B; the coda should feel earned and end with emphatic final chords.
- Because fast bowed notes sound soft in the player, the main material should live in eighths and quarters at a brisk tempo, not in sixteenth-note runs.
- Length: about 180 to 260 bars of 2/4 (or 100 to 150 of 6/8), 4 to 5 minutes. If time presses, shorten the episodes, never the ending.
EOF
for m in ii iii iv; do lor session start --title "Quartet movement $m" --working-directory quartet/ --task @briefs/$m.md 2>&1 | grep -m1 '"session_id"'; done

# Shared brief: String Quartet in D minor, "in the manner of Beethoven"

The user heard a concert, wants "more Beethoven string quartets", and asked for a full four-movement quartet by morning. I (the lead agent) am writing movement I. You write ONE other movement, complete, on your own, in the file named in your task. Work in quartet/.

## What exists
- `pieces/01-dminor-i.abc`: movement I (in progress). READ IT FIRST and copy its conventions exactly: header fields, the four `V:` lines, `%%score [1 | 2 | 3 | 4]`, the `%%MIDI program` preamble after `K:`, one line per voice per system written as `[V:1] ... |`, `%` comment lines naming each section with bar numbers, and the two first lines `%%label` (short name for the menu) and `%%note` (one sentence of programme note shown on the page).
- `check.js`: `node check.js pieces/<file>.abc` must end with `no problems found`. It checks bar lengths, that all four voices have the same number of bars, instrument ranges, and parallel fifths/octaves between any two parts (sampled every eighth note). `node check.js pieces/<file>.abc --chords --from 9 --to 16` prints the sounding notes on each beat, bottom part first; use it to confirm the harmony is what you intended. It is my substitute for ears, so use it constantly.
- The page that engraves and plays the files is abcjs 6.5.2. I build and publish; you do not.

## The quartet
- Key D minor. Middle-period Beethoven idiom (Op. 59, Op. 74, Op. 95): motivic concision, real four-part writing, dialogue between the instruments, sudden dynamic contrasts, off-beat sforzandi, silences, clear cadences and phrase structure, a real bass line. Original themes only: do not quote Beethoven or anyone else.
- The whole quartet grows from one four-note cell stated in the slow introduction of movement I: A, B flat, down a diminished seventh to C sharp, D (scale degrees 5, flat 6, raised 7, 1: semitone up, diminished seventh down, semitone up). Its major-mode form is 5, 6, 7, 1 rising by step. Your movement should use the cell or a clear transformation of it somewhere that matters (a theme head, a bass figure, a climax), not as decoration.

## Hard rules for the notation
- `L:1/8`. One meter for the whole file (check.js reads only the first `M:`). No pickup bar: start with rests inside a full first bar.
- Repeats: plain `|:` and `:|` only. No first and second endings. Write a da capo out in full.
- Tempo: `Q:"Italian marking" 1/4=NN` (or `3/8=NN` etc.). A tempo change inside the piece is an inline `[Q:"..." 1/4=NN]` in voice 1 only.
- Put every dynamic mark in all four voices (the player leaks a dynamic from one voice into the others if a voice has none). Use `!pp! !p! !mp! !mf! !f! !ff! !sfz!`, `!fermata!`, slurs `( )`, staccato `.`, `!trill!` sparingly.
- Accidentals: the key signature applies; an accidental lasts to the end of the bar in that octave; restate it after a barline. Mid-piece key signature change: inline `[K:D]` in all four voices at the same barline.
- Ranges: violins G3 (`G,`) up to about F6 (`f'`), exceptionally higher; viola C3 (`C,`) up; cello C2 (`C,,`) up. Middle C is `C`; `c` is the C above; `C,` the C below.
- Double stops `[F,A,]` are allowed but keep them rare and easy (thirds, sixths, octaves with an open string).
- Sound limits of the player: a note goes silent about 6 seconds after it starts, so no note or tied note may last longer than about 5 seconds at your tempo; re-articulate instead. Bowed samples swell slowly, so very fast notes sound soft: do not build the movement on runs of sixteenths.
- Parallel octaves that are deliberate doubling (a unison passage, two instruments in octaves on a melody for a whole phrase) are accepted by the checker when the doubling lasts; otherwise fix every flagged parallel, including those between a rocking accompaniment and a melody.

## How to work
1. Plan first, in writing for yourself: form with bar counts, keys, the themes as actual notes, the harmony bar by bar.
2. Write four to eight bars at a time for all four parts, run check.js with `--chords` on those bars, fix, go on. Do not write the whole movement before the first check.
3. Compose real music: phrases that breathe and cadence, inner parts that move, the melody passed around, the cello sometimes singing, contrast between sections, a climax, an ending that is prepared. Avoid: block chords for pages, the first violin always on top with a tune, endless sequences, a harmony that never leaves tonic and dominant.
4. Finish the whole movement to the last bar. A complete, sound movement of modest length beats an ambitious torso.

## Do not
- Edit any file except your own piece file (and scratch files under /tmp). Not check.js, template.html, build.js, publish.sh or other pieces. If check.js misbehaves on something legitimate, say so in your report instead of patching it.
- Run the browser tests or publish artifacts.

## Report back (short)
The file path; the form as a list of sections with bar numbers and keys; tempo and approximate duration; the final `node check.js` line; anything you are unsure about musically.

**Tempo:** I used `Q:"Allegro molto" 3/4=84`. abcjs accepts the dotted-half beat: it reads it as 252 quarters a minute, 714 ms per bar. With repeats it plays 264 bars, about 3 min 10 s. abcjs's player follows all the repeats.

**Form** (168 bars written):

| Bars | Section | Key | Content |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1–16, repeated | Scherzo a | D minor → F | The cell as a two-bar motto: viola and cello in octaves, answered by the violins on E, then the whole quartet. A hemiola leads to a solo D in the cello, marked p. In 9–16 the cell enters on D and on G, then a hemiola on the cell in F (C, D flat, E, F). Bar 15 is an accented F chord and bar 16 is silent. |
| 17–56, repeated | Scherzo b + a′ | B flat minor → D minor | 17–24: motto on C answered on F, then off-beat accents through B flat minor and a diminished seventh to A7. 25–28: the cell on E climbs viola → Vl. II → Vl. I over an A pedal. 29–31: hemiola with the cell in four octaves, marked ff. 33–40: only "A, B flat", pp, rising cello → Vl. I, each followed by a silent bar. 41–56 (a′): the full motto ff in four octaves, then a′ closes with a hemiola on the cell's own pitches (A B♭ C♯ D) to a D minor cadence and a silent bar. |
| 57–72, repeated | Trio c | D major | The major cell (A B C♯ D) as a legato viola tune over an open-string D–A drone in the cello. The tune then passes to Vl. I, with Vl. II in thirds below and the viola playing afterbeats. |
| 73–96, repeated | Trio d + c′ | G major → A7 → D major | The drone stops and the cello sings the cell in G, then on E towards A7. In c′ the tune is in the cello with the viola playing the drone, then Vl. I closes in D. |
| 97–152 | Scherzo da capo | D minor | Written out in full, without repeats. |
| 153–168 | Coda | D minor | The trio's rising cell in minor, pp, in cello then viola. The motto fades upward and two bars are silent. A ff hemiola on the cell over a falling bass reaches D. The cello plays "A, B flat" pp, then a unison D ff, and the last bar is a rest with a fermata. |

The last bars of the repeated sections lead both back and on as you asked: the a and b sections each end on an accented chord followed by a silent bar, and the trio ends on D major. That D major chord goes back to d (as V of G) and on to the scherzo's D minor.

Two things about playback, both tested with `setUpAudio`:
- **`!sfz!` changes nothing in playback.** The volume stays the same, and the marking prints but isn't heard. `!>!` adds about 25 to the volume, so every sforzando is written `!sfz!!>!`. This prints an accent mark next to the sfz. You may want to check movement I's sforzandi for the same problem.
- **A dynamic placed on a rest does carry over to the voice's next notes.** I relied on this so that every dynamic is in all four voices, even when a voice is resting.

Musical points I'm unsure about:
- **Silence:** a lot of it is on purpose (bars 16, 32, 34–40, 56 and their da capo, 161–162), but the 33–40 section may feel too sparse in the player.
- **Trio drone:** the cello's `[D,A,]` double stop sounds every bar for 24 bars of the trio. That is rustic, but it might sound static.
- **High notes:** in bars 27 and 123 the first violin goes up to E6/F6 at mf.
- **Repeated material:** the a′ ending and the coda's hemiola are the same idea with different basses.

**Basics**
- **Heading and tempo:** "II. Adagio molto espressivo", B flat major, 4/4, `Q:"Adagio molto espressivo" 1/4=54`.
- **Length:** 64 bars, about 4 min 45 s plus the fermatas.
- **Longest note:** 8 eighths, about 4.4 s, so under the 5-second limit. The fermatas are only on rests.
- **Conventions:** the file copies movement I's header, voices and MIDI preamble. It has `%%label` and `%%note` lines and a `%` comment naming each section with its bar numbers.

**Form**
1. **A, bars 1–20 (B flat):**
   - Bars 1–8: the hymn in the first violin's low register. Its head is F, G, A, B flat, the cell in major. Half close, then full close.
   - Bars 9–12: the second violin answers and turns to F major.
   - Bars 13–16: the hymn climbs to G5 and makes a full close.
   - Bars 17–20: the hymn's opening returns over a tonic pedal. G flat creeps in (B flat 7, then E flat minor over the B flat), and the section ends on a half close on F with a fermata.
2. **B, bars 21–40 (B flat minor, then G minor):**
   - Bars 21–28: a lament over pulsing inner parts, first in the first violin, then in the viola.
   - Bars 29–30: the intrusion. All four play F, G flat, A, B flat in octaves, ff with sfz, in the same rhythm and with the same silence as movement I's motto.
   - Bars 31–36: falling sighs in G minor, then a chromatic bass rising from G to D. At the climax the cell is on D (D, E flat, F sharp, G), now with full harmony and a diminished-seventh sfz.
   - Bars 37–40: back to F7 over a dominant pedal. The viola recalls F, G, A.
3. **A', bars 41–56 (B flat):**
   - Bars 41–48: the cello sings the hymn in its tenor register with the viola as bass. The first violin has flowing eighths, then the second violin takes them over under a quiet first-violin descant.
   - Bars 49–52: the answering phrase in the first violin, with viola triplets, turning to F.
   - Bars 53–56: the hymn's climb to its peak, with triplets continuing, and a full close.
4. **Coda, bars 57–64 (B flat), pp:**
   - Over a tonic pedal the cell sounds in major in the second violin, then in minor (with G flat) in the viola.
   - A plagal close darkened by G flat (G to G flat in the first violin).
   - Last, the cello plays F, G, A, B flat low and quietly into the final B flat chord.

**Things I'm unsure about musically**
- **Low bass under the cello's tune (bars 41–48):** the viola is the bass, and since it can't go below C3, chords that should sit on B flat are mostly in first inversion. At the bar 44 half close the cello's melody line ends on the dominant. At the bar 48 cadence the cello drops a ninth from its melody C to the low B flat to supply the root.
- **The middle section:** it's mostly two-beat sighs and off-beat pulses. The checker accepts it, but it may sound static.
- **Climax (bars 35–36):** it's brief, two bars and then silence, like the motto. It may need more lead-in.
- **Pulse texture (bars 21–28):** the off-beat eighths in the inner parts (the violins in bars 25–28) are written as `z!p!DDD`, with the dynamic on the first note after the rest. abcjs reports no warnings, but I haven't heard how the player renders them.
- **Viola triplets (bars 49–56):** check.js snaps triplet notes to the eighth grid, so its parallel-fifths and octaves check only partly covers these bars.

**Movement IV is finished:** `quartet/pieces/04-dminor-iv.abc`, 197 bars of 2/4 (in your 180–260 range). The last line of `node check.js pieces/04-dminor-iv.abc` is `no problems found`, and all four voices have 197 bars.

**Tempo and length:** `Q:"Allegro con fuoco" 1/4=100`, then `[Q:"Presto" 1/4=144]` at the coda. That comes to about 3¾ minutes with the fermatas, a little under your 4–5 minutes. Setting the opening tempo to about 1/4=92 would reach 4 minutes without adding bars; I kept 100 so the gallop stays brisk.

**Form** (rondo, D minor):
- **Refrain A, bars 1–24 (D minor).** The refrain tune is the cell plus a neighbour note: A, B♭, A, down to C♯, D, in a quarter–eighth–eighth gallop. The first violin plays it over off-beat pulses. Bars 13–14 put the cell on G, bars 17–20 are the motto in four octaves, ff, and a cadence and silence close the section.
- **Transition, bars 25–32.** The tune's head is in the viola, then the cell on C (C, D♭, E, F) leads to the dominant of F, with a fermata.
- **Episode B, bars 33–64 (F major).** A hymn whose first four notes are the cell's major form on C. The first violin states it, then the cello sings it in its tenor register with the viola as bass, then the violins repeat it quietly over pulsing inner parts. Bars 57–64 climb through G minor and A to the original cell, ff.
- **Retransition, bars 65–76.** An A pedal, the tune's head passed up from viola to first violin, off-beat sforzandi on A7, silence.
- **Refrain A′, bars 77–100.** The tune an octave lower in the viola, then back in the first violin over driving eighths. This time the cadence breaks off on B♭ (deceptive), with a fermata.
- **Episode C, bars 101–143.**
  - Bars 101–118: fugato on the subject (the cell in quarters plus an eighth-note tail). It enters in the cello (D minor), viola (answer in A minor), second violin and first violin.
  - Bars 119–126: the tail passed between the violins down a circle of fifths.
  - Bars 127–134: the cell in augmentation in the cello, rising chromatically to A.
  - Bars 135–143: climax with the cell in long notes in octave violins over a falling bass, then a Neapolitan chord, A7 and silence.
- **Refrain A″, bars 144–165.** Forte, the violins in octaves, then louder. It halts on A7 with a fermata.
- **Coda, bars 166–197 (`[K:D]`, Presto).**
  - Bars 166–173: the tune turned major, so the cell rises by step (A, B, A, C♯, D), first in the second violin, then the first.
  - Bars 174–181: the cello sings it under off-beat chords.
  - Bars 182–189: everyone plays it ff in octaves over a galloping bass.
  - Bars 190–197: A, B, C♯, D in long notes in the cello under a falling first violin, then D–A–D–D chords. The last chord is the file's only double stops (open-string fifths in viola and cello, a sixth in the second violin).

**What I'm unsure about musically:**
- **Fugato texture (bars 101–118):** only two or three parts play, with some bare fifths and octaves. It reads as a sketch of counterpoint, not real three- or four-part fugue writing.
- **Thin beats in bars 127–134:** the accompaniment is on the off-beats, so on the beat often only the cello and one violin sound.
- **Repeated return:** bars 152–159 repeat 85–92 with only the dynamics raised. The other two refrain returns are really varied (viola lead at 77, violins in octaves at 144, deceptive cadence at 99).
- **Climax line:** in bars 135–138 the cell rises A, B♭, C♯, D with an augmented second, not the diminished-seventh leap. I meant that as tension before the major coda, but it's a judgement call.
- **High coda line:** the first violin goes up to G6 in bars 190–192, which may sound shrill in the player.

I only edited my own piece file; earlier versions are in `/tmp/iv-*.abc`.

- **Climax line:** in bars 135–138 the cell rises A, B♭, C♯, D with an augmented second, not the diminished-seventh leap. I meant that as tension before the major coda, but it's a judgement call.
- **High coda line:** the first violin goes up to G6 in bars 190–192, which may sound shrill in the player.

I only edited my own piece file; earlier versions are in `/tmp/iv-*.abc`.

open(p,'w').write('\n'.join(L))

- **One high point.** I lowered the first violin in 131 and 133–134, which removed the passing F6 in bar 133. Nothing before the coda now goes above the Neapolitan E♭6 at bar 139 (a pitch the refrain itself reaches at bars 13, 89 and 156). The coda's G6 is the last peak.
- **Part-writing fixes:**
  - Doubled leading tone (C♯ in two parts over A) removed at 88 and 155, and at 126 on a half-cadence chord.
  - Doubled G♯ removed at 116.
  - Bar 117 is now a proper E7 over G♯, going to D minor over F.
  - Chordal sevenths now resolve down: viola in 39 (no longer moves B♭ to C), and in 62 (G4 to F4, with a full D minor over F).
  - The B♭ chord with no fifth at 44 now has its F.

**What I left, and why:**
- **Fugato exposition (101–110).** It stays at one voice, then two. That thinness is normal in a fugue exposition, and four parts are reached at 115.
- **The augmented second at 135–137** (B♭ to C♯ in long notes). It is the cell rising at the climax, so it is the point.
- **Cello above the viola at 41–48.** This is deliberate: the cello sings the hymn in its tenor register.
- **First violin more than an octave above the second at 190–193.** This is a four-bar flourish over the final cadence.
- **Dominant seventh with no resolution before a silence** (bars 141–142, before the refrain returns) and at 165 (before the coda). These are breaks between sections.
- **Proportions.** Refrain about 24 bars, B 32, C 43, coda 32 (Presto); I judged each long enough to register. The final cadence is prepared: the bass rises A–B–C♯–D (5 to 1), then D–A–D–D chords.

**Length:** still about 3¾ minutes, short of the 4–5 the first brief asked for. You said not to stretch it much, so I didn't add bars. Setting the opening tempo to 1/4=92 would reach about 4 minutes.

I've finished the revision pass on `pieces/02-dminor-ii.abc`. It now has 65 bars (one more), about 4 min 50 s, and `node check.js pieces/02-dminor-ii.abc` ends with `no problems found`. I've only checked it with the checker's chord printouts, not by listening. The pre-revision file is saved at `/tmp/ii-before-rev.abc`.

**What I changed**
- **Climax lead-in and high point (bars 33–37, one bar added):**
  - The chromatic bass now rises over three bars (G A | B♭ B | C C♯) to the D, with the marks building mp, mf, f, ff.
  - Bar 33 is now G minor going to D7/A (V4/3), which leads into G minor/B♭.
  - The first violin climbs (D C | D F | E♭ G G B♭) into the cell on D an octave higher (D6, E♭6, F♯6, G6), with the second violin doubling it an octave below. The viola has easy double stops under it.
  - G6 is now the movement's single highest note; the next highest is the B♭5 in bar 56.
  - Both sforzandi (bars 29 and 36) are written `!sfz!!>!`.
- **Static B section (bars 25–28):** the first violin's pulsing is replaced by a counterline (F, D | E♭, C | B♭, D B♭ | C, A) above the viola's lament. The second violin keeps pulsing.
- **Copied return (bars 55–56):** the reprise of the hymn's climb now runs through eighths (B♭ C | D E♭ F G) up to B♭5 instead of repeating bars 14–15.
- **Bar 49 cadence:** the cello now goes B♭3, F3, B♭2, so its tune resolves to B♭3 before it drops to the root.
- **Part-writing fixes from the `--chords` audit:**
  - **Bar 3:** the bass now goes E♭, F, G (V to vi) instead of the tritone drop E♭ to A.
  - **Sevenths that didn't resolve down by step:** fixed in bars 3, 11, 14, 20, 23, 26, 32–33, 40, 42–43, 47, 52 and 55.
  - **Doubled leading tone:** fixed in bars 42, 45 and 56.
  - **Bar 12:** the viola's E♭ is gone. Bar 20's F7 is held so its E♭ resolves to the D♭ of bar 21.
  - **Parallels:** fixing the above created new parallels, and I re-voiced the figuration in bars 42–47 to remove them.

**What I left, and why**
- **Bars 9–12:** this four-bar answer is in three parts, with the first violin silent. It's deliberate dialogue and the voice-leading is sound.
- **Bars 42–49, viola as bass:** keeping the cello in its tenor register needs this, and the cadences are now sound.
- **Bar 46, beat 4:** the chord has no root (A, C, E♭, a vii° chord leading to G minor). It's acceptable.
- **No-fifth chords:** bars 7, 35 and 43 each have a chord with no fifth on a beat. The thirds are all present.
- **Bars 9–12 and 50–53 match** (the answering phrase). The orchestration differs: second violin first, then first violin over viola triplets.
- **Proportions:** A runs 20 bars, B 21, A′ 16 and the coda 8. The coda's ending (plagal close with G♭, then the cell low in the cello) still sounds prepared and final to me.

**Still unverified**
- **Viola triplets:** check.js snaps them to the eighth-note grid, so its parallel-fifth and octave check only partly covers them.
- **Climax volume:** I haven't checked how the doubled G6 sounds in the player.

Final line: `no problems found`.

- **Copied return (bars 55–56):** the reprise of the hymn's climb now runs through eighths (B♭ C | D E♭ F G) up to B♭5 instead of repeating bars 14–15.
- **Bar 49 cadence:** the cello now goes B♭3, F3, B♭2, so its tune resolves to B♭3 before it drops to the root.
- **Part-writing fixes from the `--chords` audit:**
  - **Bar 3:** the bass now goes E♭, F, G (V to vi) instead of the tritone drop E♭ to A.
  - **Sevenths that didn't resolve down by step:** fixed in bars 3, 11, 14, 20, 23, 26, 32–33, 40, 42–43, 47, 52 and 55.
  - **Doubled leading tone:** fixed in bars 42, 45 and 56.
  - **Bar 12:** the viola's E♭ is gone. Bar 20's F7 is held so its E♭ resolves to the D♭ of bar 21.
  - **Parallels:** fixing the above created new parallels, and I re-voiced the figuration in bars 42–47 to remove them.

**What I left, and why**
- **Bars 9–12:** this four-bar answer is in three parts, with the first violin silent. It's deliberate dialogue and the voice-leading is sound.
- **Bars 42–49, viola as bass:** keeping the cello in its tenor register needs this, and the cadences are now sound.
- **Bar 46, beat 4:** the chord has no root (A, C, E♭, a vii° chord leading to G minor). It's acceptable.
- **No-fifth chords:** bars 7, 35 and 43 each have a chord with no fifth on a beat. The thirds are all present.
- **Bars 9–12 and 50–53 match** (the answering phrase). The orchestration differs: second violin first, then first violin over viola triplets.
- **Proportions:** A runs 20 bars, B 21, A′ 16 and the coda 8. The coda's ending (plagal close with G♭, then the cell low in the cello) still sounds prepared and final to me.

**Still unverified**
- **Viola triplets:** check.js snaps them to the eighth-note grid, so its parallel-fifth and octave check only partly covers them.
- **Climax volume:** I haven't checked how the doubled G6 sounds in the player.

The full quartet is written: four movements, about 18 minutes, all in the player above. Press play on the first movement and it runs on through the other three.

Nobody has heard it yet. I can't listen, so every check was by analysis, and you are the first audience.

| Movement | Key and form | Bars | Length |
|---|---|---|---|
| I. Poco sostenuto. Allegro agitato | D minor, slow introduction and sonata form | 153 | 6:22 |
| II. Adagio molto espressivo | B♭ major, hymn with a dark middle | 65 | 4:49 |
| III. Scherzo. Allegro molto | D minor, trio in D major | 168 | 3:09 |
| IV. Allegro con fuoco. Presto | D minor rondo with a fugato, D major coda | 197 | 3:45 |

The whole quartet grows from the four-note cell you heard last night (A, B♭, down to C♯, D). It is the motto of the first movement, the head of the hymn in its major form, the scherzo's motive, and the finale's refrain and fugue subject. In the last coda it finally rises by step in D major.

I wrote the first movement myself. Three subagents each wrote one of the other movements in parallel from a shared brief, and each then did one revision pass on its own movement.

**What was checked**
- **Notation:** every bar has the right length, all four parts line up, and every note is within its instrument's range.
- **Part-writing:** no parallel fifths or octaves between any two parts, and the revision pass fixed unresolved sevenths and doubled leading tones in movements II to IV.
- **Player:** each movement renders to audio without clipping, and playback moves on to the next movement at the end.

**Where I expect weaknesses**
- **The sound:** these are sampled strings with no vibrato control or real bowing. Fast passages and the pulsing accompaniments will sound mechanical. Short notes are boosted to compensate for the slow attack, and I can't tell whether that sounds natural.
- **Finale fugato (bars 101–118):** it is thin, two or three parts with some bare intervals.
- **Finale length:** it is short for a last movement.
- **Scherzo silences:** there are many deliberate silent bars, which may feel like holes in this player.
- **Adagio triplets (bars 50–57):** the parallel-motion check only partly covers them.

The player has a few additions since last night: a menu of the four movements, the instruments spread left to right, and audible sforzando accents.

When you've listened, tell me what works and what doesn't, by movement and bar number if you can (the status line shows the bar as it plays). I can revise from that. I can also put the page on GitHub Pages for a shareable URL, or export MIDI or MusicXML for notation software.

Listen to the quartetScores & source

The composition notebook

How Beethoven’s Missing Quartet was written, revised, and made playable.

An original AI-composed homage in D minor, not a rediscovered Beethoven work. Composed on November 14, 2026.

This is an edited, high-level account of the composition process, based on the recorded briefs, completion reports, score revisions, and test results. It is not a verbatim transcript or a disclosure of private internal reasoning. The musical judgments are analytical: the agents did not listen to the performance.

One small cell links four movements

The starting idea was to write a new quartet inspired by Beethoven’s middle-period language: concentrated motives, dialogue between instruments, abrupt changes of dynamics, and silences that interrupt an otherwise clear phrase.

A   B♭   C♯   D

A semitone up, a diminished seventh down, then a semitone up.

The minor-mode cell is transformed rather than quoted mechanically. Its major counterpart rises by step: A–B–C♯–D. That transformation connects the slow movement’s hymn, the scherzo’s trio, and the finale’s D-major coda.

One lead agent wrote movement I and built the player. Three subagents each wrote a different movement from a shared musical brief, then made a revision pass. The lead integrated the scores and checked their playback.

Each movement gives the cell a different role

I. Poco sostenuto. Allegro agitato

153 bars · approximately 6:22 · D minor · sonata form

The slow introduction introduces the cell from the cello upward through all four instruments. The Allegro turns it into a fortissimo octave motto, interrupted by quiet answers. A singing second theme moves to F major; the development darkens it and passes the cell through imitative entries.

The reprise briefly offers D major before the minor motto interrupts it. The coda remembers the slow introduction, then closes emphatically in D minor.

Revision and playback decisions

Flagged parallels were re-voiced in the accompaniment and cadences. The slow introduction’s tied notes were shortened by re-articulating them, because the sampled strings stop sustaining after about six seconds. Key changes needed a player fix to preserve the viola and cello clefs.

Read the ABC score

II. Adagio molto espressivo

65 bars · approximately 4:49 · B♭ major · A–B–A′ with coda

The opening hymn uses the cell’s major form: F–G–A–B♭. The middle section turns to B♭ minor and G minor, with the minor cell intruding in octaves. On the return, the cello sings the hymn in its tenor register while the viola supplies the bass.

What changed in the revision

One bar was added to prepare the climax: a chromatic bass now climbs G–A–B♭–B–C–C♯ toward D. Pulsing notes above the viola’s lament became a counterline. The returning hymn was decorated rather than simply copied, and the cello’s cadence was reshaped to resolve the melody before dropping to the bass.

The part-writing pass also changed unresolved sevenths and doubled leading tones. The viola’s triplets remain only partly covered by the automated parallel-motion check, which samples on an eighth-note grid.

Read the ABC score

III. Scherzo. Allegro molto

168 written bars, with repeats · approximately 3:09 · D minor; D-major trio

The cell becomes a terse two-bar gesture, thrown between instruments with displaced accents, hemiolas, and sudden gaps. The trio turns it into a rustic rising tune over a D–A drone. The scherzo returns, written out rather than left as a da-capo instruction.

What changed in the revision

A quiet cello pedal was added beneath the sparse fragments in bars 33–40 and their return. The trio’s drone now yields to dominant-to-tonic bass motion at its cadences. In the coda, two silent bars became an accented dominant preparation before the final outburst.

Some silence was deliberately retained: a strong cadence followed by nothing is part of the scherzo’s character. Several chordal sevenths and incomplete cadences were also corrected.

Read the ABC score

IV. Allegro con fuoco. Presto

197 bars · approximately 3:45 · D-minor rondo; D-major coda

A galloping refrain transforms the cell into A–B♭–A–C♯–D. A hymn-like F-major episode contrasts with it, and a later fugato gives the cell successive entries. The last coda turns the refrain major and quickens to Presto.

What changed in the revision

A repeated refrain return now begins quietly and rebuilds, with the second violin shadowing the tune instead of merely pulsing. Sustained viola notes fill out the approach to the climax, whose dynamics now rise in stages. The ending retains its high first-violin flourish over the rising major-mode cell in the bass.

The fugato still begins thinly, and the finale is shorter than originally planned. Those are places to revisit after listening, not defects an automated check can settle.

Read the ABC score

The player needed as much testing as the score

ABC notation stores each score as editable text. abcjs engraves it and builds a performance from instrument samples. Several problems were reproduced and fixed during development:

  • Silent playback: instrument choices were being changed after the library selected its samples, and numeric instrument IDs replaced names. Selecting programs earlier restored sound.
  • Resume and seek: pause did not reset the library’s toggle state; seeking also left a stale start time. The transport was changed to pause, seek, then resume in the correct order.
  • Missing accents: a bare !sfz! printed but did not change note velocity. An explicit accent was added alongside it.
  • Slow string attacks: short bowed notes were much quieter than long notes. The player gives them a bounded level boost; the artistic effect still needs human listening.
  • Clipping: loud passages exceeded full scale. The rendered stereo buffer is scaled to a peak of 0.9 before playback.

Checks are evidence, not a verdict on the music

All four final scores passed the project’s structural checks: matching bar counts, bar durations, instrument ranges, and its sampled parallel-fifths-and-octaves test. The parser reported no warnings. Headless-browser tests produced non-silent buffers for every movement, with no samples exceeding full scale after normalization.

Those checks do not prove that the counterpoint is flawless or that the quartet succeeds musically. Deliberate octave doubling is exempted; triplets and double stops are incompletely represented in the parallel checker. Phrasing, balance, idiomatic bowing, and the sense of a convincing large-scale argument remain matters for performers and listeners.

The first user confirmed that playback was audible. No agent judged the completed quartet by ear. If something feels static, too abrupt, or unconvincing, the score is meant to be revised—not defended by a passing test.

Sources for this account: the recorded composition briefs, movement-completion and revision reports, score comments, and browser/audio test outputs. Summarized and edited for public reading; raw private chat logs are not included.

An original AI-composed string quartet in D minor, inspired by Beethoven. **Not a lost or rediscovered work by Beethoven.** Composed with Lor in four movements; approximately 18 minutes.

In **Settings → Pages**, choose **Deploy from a branch**, select **main**, choose **/ (root)**, and save.

The site will be at https://akrentsel.github.io/beethovens-missing-quartet/ once deployment finishes.

The page needs network access for the notation library, fonts and instrument samples. Click Play to enable browser audio. The scores and player have been checked analytically and in headless-browser tests; this is not a recording of live performers or a musicological claim about what Beethoven would have written.
